title: The Twilight of Oil in an Age of Uncertainty: From a Vicious to a Virtuous Cycle
author: Nur  Arafeh
text:
Source: GettyPaperMalcolm H. Kerr Carnegie Middle East CenterThe Twilight of Oil in an Age of Uncertainty: From a Vicious to a Virtuous CycleThe global hydrocarbon order is changing. Economic diversification and developing productive economies have become essential for Middle Eastern and North African states, requiring them to address social and political challenges and rethink domestic, regional, and global settlements.Link CopiedBy Nur Arafeh, Ishac Diwan, Hamza Meddeb, Marwan MuasherPublished on Oct 30, 2026This paper was written with insights from the following commission members: Muna Abbas, Mohammed Abdel Raouf, Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, Youssef Al-Ebraheem, Ziad BahaEddin, Ferid Belhaj, Noha El Mikawy, Rima Khalaf, Ali Kooli, Slim Othmani, Tarik Youssef, and Maha Yahya. AcknowledgmentsThis paper is a product of workshops and online sessions that have been held over the past two years with a commission of regional experts, chaired by Marwan Muasher. The authors gratefully acknowledge the Asfari Foundation’s generous support for this project.IntroductionThe Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region has been a major producer and exporter of hydrocarbons since the 1930s. In 2025, around 30 percent of global hydrocarbon exports originated in the MENA region, with collective regional revenues amounting to over $1 trillion.1 Since 2000, when the second oil boom began (the first being in October 1973), MENA has sold $25 trillion worth of oil and gas (adjusted for 2025 prices). As demonstrated by the conflict between the United States and Iran, events in the region remain consequential for international energy markets. But equally, hydrocarbons have shaped the region’s economies, governance structures, and societies in ways that now define the nature of the challenge ahead.The challenge in question is one of fundamental economic transformation. The global hydrocarbons order is facing profound change, as environmental and geopolitical pressures undermine the foundations on which many MENA economies have rested. In this context, economic diversification is no longer optional; it has become both strategic and urgent. Yet diversification is not merely a technical exercise. It brings with it at least three types of fundamental and interconnected challenges. The first is economic, and involves countries determining how to increase their labor productivity and build sustainable productive capacity outside hydrocarbons in economies long structured around resource rents. The second challenge is social and political, affecting how to renegotiate social contracts that support more inclusive societies. The third is regional, where the success or failure of transformation will depend not only on domestic reform, but on whether a more stable regional order can emerge, one in which economic cooperation prevails over conflict, fragmentation, and escalating tensions. Escaping the current vicious cycle and turning it into a virtuous one is essential for the region’s future.This paper does not offer a single prescription and acknowledges that the MENA region encompasses countries at very different stages of development, with very different resource endowments, institutional capacities, and political settlements. The analysis focuses on three groups of countries: high-income hydrocarbon exporters (Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries), middle-income hydrocarbon exporters (Algeria, Iraq, Libya, and Iran), and middle-income hydrocarbon importers (Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Morocco, and Tunisia). We offer an integrated approach to the economic, political, and regional dimensions of the diversification imperative and the need to strengthen productivity, as well as policy recommendations organized around the five key questions that structured the commission’s deliberations.The first question is the most fundamental one: Why must MENA countries diversify, and why now? For all the countries examined here, the answer is that, for various reasons, the demand for hydrocarbons is falling in a world shaped by a volatile energy transition and a pressing imperative of energy security. This will inexorably reduce oil and gas exports and revenues over the medium to long term, sharply constraining these countries’ access to foreign exchange and deepening their fiscal pressures. Many of the hydrocarbon exporting countries understand therefore that, because they will not be able to finance employment of their growing labor force in the public sector, they must immediately begin investing in productive jobs if they are to meet future challenges. Energy importers face a different challenge: They realize that it will be impossible in the coming years to export carbon-intensive manufactured goods to Europe as carbon border adjustment mechanisms and other environmental regulations take effect. The war with Iran has exacerbated such tensions. For one thing, oil revenues will fall more rapidly, implying a need to diversify more rapidly. Additionally, the war is likely to force changes in the way in which diversification takes place. The oil importing countries, especially Egypt, Jordan, and Lebanon, will sustain indirect losses, which is one more reason why they need to try harder to improve their labor productivity through growth-enhancing reforms.The second question concerns the current state of play: What is the situation when it comes to diversification efforts in the MENA region? The picture is highly uneven:GCC countries are heavily engaged in investing in productivity and diversification, but the results remain mixed. The most dynamic sectors have been oil products, entrepôt trade, tourism, hospitality, entertainment, and more recently renewables and artificial intelligence (AI) centers.2 However, generating productive jobs has been challenging, and the globally oriented model that underpins Gulf diversification strategies is threated by regional instability. The ability of the GCC countries to navigate a turbulent global energy transition is also in jeopardy.Among the middle-income hydrocarbon exporters (Iraq, Algeria, Libya, Iran), the pattern is one of rent consumption rather than investment. Productivity growth is absent, rent per capita is falling, and there is as yet no credible exit path from this trajectory.Middle-income hydrocarbon importers present an equally troubling picture, as they have been stuck in a severe form of the middle-income trap: They are operating below potential, with fragile social and financial situations, and are failing to pursue growth-enhancing reforms. Savings are low, as is investment, underemployment is rampant, and these countries each face a brewing debt crisis, while state services have been severely rolled back. The main problem is an unbalanced form of capitalism dominated by a closed economic elite that is unwilling to allow space for competition from firms not under its control. Political connections are based on loyalty, not productivity, which represents a key obstacle to transformation.The third question is political. What are the social and political implications of the current trajectory? Across the MENA region, the social contracts that offered material provision in exchange for political acquiescence are under mounting strain. The generation now entering the labor market is better educated than its predecessors, holds higher aspirations, and has grown up with direct exposure to different global living standards. However, it also faces higher unemployment than preceding generations, deteriorating public services, and more precarious labor markets. The nature of this strain diverges across country groups, reflecting fundamentally different distributional bargains. In the GCC, the rentier bargain is being restructured through nationalization of the labor force and subsidy reform, generating grievances with few formal outlets to express them.3 In middle-income hydrocarbon exporting countries, revenues sustain narrow patronage networks, but cannot finance mass consumption or broad legitimacy. In hydrocarbon importing states, such as Egypt and Jordan, external geopolitical rents that once underpinned the social contract are being eroded, leaving governments with shrinking fiscal space and facing rising social instability.What unites all three country groups is the dilemma of how to deal with the fact that the reforms needed to build productive diversified economies are politically costly in the short run, even as inaction is economically unsustainable in the long run. Faced with this dilemma, governments have responded across the board by centralizing power and intensifying control, either to manage reform (in the case of the GCC countries) or avoid it (in the case of other states, such as Algeria, Egypt, Jordan, and Tunisia). However, this approach is straining the very foundations on which a durable economic transformation must rest—rule of law, investor confidence, legitimate channels for objection. The difficulties reformist politicians are facing are complex. They must propose attractive reforms that generate support from a coalition of reformist parties or pressure groups, create mechanisms that compensate losers and bring them into the fold, put in place checks and balances to avoid costly mistakes and learn from experience, and finally permit the voicing of grievances to avoid the type of explosion that was common during the decade of Arab uprisings.The fourth question concerns the external environment. How do regional and global dynamics shape, and potentially undermine, diversification efforts? Falling hydrocarbon revenues will intensify regional competition in the oil and gas market if it is not matched by improved regional cooperation, as countries seek to defend their share of a shrinking market. This reality has become more acute since the beginning of the war with Iran, which dampened global appetite for Gulf oil and gas due to elevated perceived risks. Moreover, increased insecurity has also disrupted Gulf diversification strategies in areas that are highly sensitive to security conditions—foreign direct investment, tourism, or trade.In this more volatile environment, countries need to imagine growth paths that are more resilient to shocks and less likely to generate them. This requires building regional economic interdependencies, which today remain underdeveloped. It would mean expanding intraregional trade and investment, advancing a regional security architecture that reduces business risk and lessens reliance on any single external guarantor, and diversifying external economic relationships in a world increasingly organized around geopolitical blocs. To be able to sustain diversified relations, stronger regional bargaining power helps. This could come in the form of more robust soft power derived from better management of regional public goods such as defending the environment, improving security, caring for refugees, and preventing states from failing. There are other arguments for improved regional cooperation in the form of the growth of a regional market: the need to bring some accumulated savings in the form of globally placed Sovereign Wealth Funds’ assets closer to home, given rising expropriation risks; the fact that environmental challenges are regional; and the advisability of preserving and diversifying regional trade routes.The fifth and final question is a holistic one: How do these elements interact, and under what conditions can the region move from a vicious to a virtuous cycle? The elements discussed above can interact positively or negatively. The status quo increases regional tensions, political risk, and doom loops—or self-reinforcing cycles that exacerbate problems—of economic decline and violence. The overlapping aspects of the transition—economic, social, political, and environmental—create structural tensions, but progress on one front can create momentum for broader reforms and a virtuous cycle that facilitates progress:A regional security deal would be much enhanced by regional economic cooperation. Moreover, the financial rates of return to the region of sovereign wealth fund investment would be greater if invested in large rather than small markets. Cooperation is also needed to fight climate change.The ability to implement industrial policy to develop new value chains in a secure regional environment would enable the region to bargain for a fairer role in a fragmented world order.Reduced regional instability and the development of a regional market would create positive incentives for recalcitrant regimes to invest in growth, especially in middle-income countries.Insufficient Progress in Productivity and DiversificationWhile some hydrocarbon exporters have made progress on diversification, they mostly remain insufficiently diversified. Oil importers, for their part, have achieved only low levels of labor productivity. As a result, diversification should be an important aim for oil and gas exporters, and oil importers should target efficiency gains with more determination. At the same time, there are many ways in which the world is changing, which offer additional reasons for accelerating diversification and efficiency efforts.In absolute terms, countries with larger oil and gas revenues per capita have managed to diversify their economy more than those with lower levels of revenue.The Appeal and Challenge of Economic DiversificationFor the past fifty years, oil and gas revenues have enriched Middle Eastern countries. Hydrocarbons have financed the building of modern states, infrastructures, and social services. In some but not all oil and gas producing countries, these revenues have also supported the development of productive private sectors beyond fossil fuels. Paradoxically, in absolute terms, countries with larger oil and gas revenues per capita have managed to diversify their economy more than those with lower levels of revenue (see figure 1). The United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Qatar have the highest levels of hydrocarbon revenues per capita, though these revenues have come to constitute a small share of their countries’ total GDP. This reflects their wide-ranging diversification into non-oil and gas sectors as well as financial earnings from their sovereign wealth fund. In contrast, in Iraq and Algeria, hydrocarbons revenues are relatively modest on a per capita basis, but they constitute a large share of GDP, as national production outside hydrocarbons remains modest.
Most economies in the region remain highly dependent on hydrocarbons in two additional dimensions of their economic structure—fiscal revenues and exports (see figure 2). In Oman, Qatar, Kuwait, and Iraq, the share of hydrocarbon revenues as a proportion both of state revenues and exports is close to or above 80 percent. Other countries are making progress in diversifying either revenue sources or exports, or both. For example, Bahrain has diversified its exports more than any other GCC country, with 50 percent of its exports being non-hydrocarbon. Saudi Arabia and Algeria now receive around 40 percent of their state revenues from non-hydrocarbons. The UAE has made progress on both fronts: 30 percent of its exports and 60 percent of its state revenues are from non-hydrocarbon sources.Hydrocarbon producers have long aspired to diversify their economies, and there are good reasons for accelerating this process. The end of the global thirst for hydrocarbon consumption can now be seen on the horizon. This will not happen because of oil and gas running out, but rather because of an inexorable fall in demand, which will reduce the MENA region’s hydrocarbon revenues over the medium to long term. Global demand for oil and gas from the region is predicted to recede over time for three reasons: technological change will impose a reduction; the climate transition will push countries to cut back on carbon-dioxide emissions; and risks specific to the Middle East might deter oil and gas companies and producers from investing in new reserves in the region. It is also difficult to predict the speed of this decline in revenue, since it will depend not just on global demand, but also on oil and gas prices and the share the region will retain of global demand. Technological change: Hydrocarbons, which are mainly being used to fuel vehicles, are being overtaken by alternative types of energy. In the past ten years, the expanded use of electrical automobiles, which run on electricity produced from various sources—nuclear, hydro, solar and wind, as well as biofuels, gas, and coal—has been rapid. The development of battery technologies has allowed the prices of electrical vehicles to reach parity with vehicles that have internal combustion engines, something that will affect future hydrocarbon demand. These developments have been in large part driven by China, which is keen to capture a new global market in renewables, but also to secure its own energy autonomy. Beijing has made a determined and increasingly successful effort to wean itself off imported fuel. Between 2022 and 2025, China emerged as the main producer and exporter of advanced and competitive renewable energy technology.4 As of 2025, the country dominated solar, wind, and battery technology, and was exporting cost-competitive alternatives to oil and gas on a global scale. Climate transition: The 2015 Paris agreement, signed by 196 countries, committed the signatories to ensuring that global temperatures would not rise more than 1.5°C by reducing greenhouse gas emissions.5 While the exact path and speed of the global temperature increase remain uncertain, because hydrocarbons are major carbon-dioxide producers, their consumption will have to be curtailed. Admittedly, the collective commitment to a rapid reduction in the carbon-dioxide footprint has been weakened in Europe, and especially in the United States, because of budgetary pressures and mounting opposition from constituencies that stand to lose out. Nevertheless, technological progress and geopolitical divergences are creating new incentives to avoid depending on oil and gas and to develop renewable energies.Wars and insecurity: The consequences of the Iran war have lessened the desirability of purchasing Middle Eastern oil. If the risks do not decrease significantly, global demand for oil from the region may fall more precipitously. This would be ironic, given that hydrocarbon production in the Gulf is the cheapest in the world. The Gulf states had counted on benefitting from this advantage to remain the last global producers of oil and gas, but geographical risks are increasing transport and insurance costs in ways that neutralize geological advantage.Recent estimates by the International Energy Agency (IEA) illustrate the possible magnitude of the fall in hydrocarbon revenues.6 The IEA presents three scenarios: Net Zero Emissions by 2050 (NZE), as per the Paris agreements; an Announced Pledges Scenario (APS), which assumes that all climate commitments as of August 2023 are fully met on time; and a Stated Transition Energy Policy Scenario (STEPS), which reflects the energy policies that were in place as of August 2023 (see figure 3 and box 1). In the NZE and APS reform scenarios, global oil demand is projected to fall by 50 to 75 percent by 2050—enormous shifts compared to the status quo STEPS scenario. Change is already in motion, as reflected by the steep fall in investment in new oil and gas capacity, and an equally steep rise in investment in renewable capacity worldwide. This is especially true of the United States, the European Union, and China, which together dominate renewable energy production. Total revenues accruing to oil and gas producers are projected to decline rapidly under the NZE and APS scenarios. Currently, production in the MENA region represents around 38 percent of global production. In the reform scenarios, GCC revenues are expected to fall precipitously, even if they may manage to increase their share of smaller global demand, due to lower extraction costs (the dashed line scenarios in figure 3). Even in the status quo scenario, the revenues of the states in the MENA region are also projected to fall, albeit by much less, due to reduced demand and lower prices.A second reason for countries to diversify relates to population growth and the rise in education. These two factors require economies in the MENA region to generate more and better jobs for their populations. But oil and gas rents per capita have declined since 2010. This is in part due to a drop in prices, which stabilized at around $60 per barrel before the Iran war (a figure that is expected to fall further following a permanent end to hostilities). But the decline in per capita rents is also very much due to demographic pressures that will continue to progressively increase the fiscal cost of redistribution (see figure 4).
Most importantly, population growth and progress in education mean it is no longer possible to hire all educated citizens for government jobs, as in the early days of oil and gas. In many hydrocarbon-producing countries, secondary education is near universal and nearly half of all graduates acquire a university degree.7 Integrating them all into the public sector is not just onerous for the state, it represents a highly inefficient use of their potential. This new challenge requires creating jobs outside the bureaucracy, in productive activities.
This is particularly true for countries already running high fiscal deficits, such as Algeria, Bahrain, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia, all of which have had a hard time maintaining around 40 percent of labor in the public sector and trying to balance their books with oil below $100 per barrel (see figure 5). Kuwait’s challenge is even more daunting, as the country still employs over 80 percent of its national workforce in the public sector, which requires large fiscal expenditures, producing fiscal deficits unless oil and gas prices remain at an elevated level. Only Qatar, the UAE, and Oman can afford to pay for large public sectors, even at low oil and gas prices. As hydrocarbon revenues must be invested to prepare for the hoped-for, productive non-hydrocarbon economy of tomorrow, a growing share of state budgets must come from other sources, such as taxation. More ambitiously, the decline in oil and gas revenues requires developing new sources of exports to continue generating foreign exchange as revenues shrink.The third rationale for diversification into productive activities is to create opportunities to invest the region’s savings closer to home, given the rising risks posed by an increasingly volatile world. In such a context, investing in diversification reduces the dangers to a country’s financial assets. Currently, 42 percent of the sovereign wealth funds of GCC states are invested in the United States and 32 percent in Europe (see figure 6). Yet both regions have extremely elevated ratios of public debt to GDP, something that presages high risks of macroeconomic and foreign exchange instability. In contrast, only 19 percent of the sovereign wealth fund resources are invested in Asia. And only a very small share is invested in the MENA region: No more than 3 percent of sovereign wealth fund resources are invested in the GCC and 4 percent in the rest of the Middle East. From a diversification perspective, it would make sense to invest a larger share in Asia and the Middle East. Investing in the MENA region today may seem risky, but in a longer-term perspective it can contribute to fueling higher growth and enhancing regional security though interdependencies, thereby improving the long-term security of savings for future generations.

Box 1. The Future of Demand for Middle Eastern Oil. 
Karen E. Young
The IEA’s World Energy Outlook 2025 finds that oil will remain the dominant fuel until 2050 if current policies remain in place. Growth would be largely a Global South phenomenon—India, Asia, the Middle East, and Africa account for the bulk of long-term demand growth, with India alone adding 8.2 mb/d, while OECD demand is expected to fall by 8.5 mb/d. Gas is the fastest-growing hydrocarbon, driven substantially by AI data center electricity demand.
The Iran war may incentivize countries to reduce oil demand across their transportation sectors more rapidly. This short-term disruption could have much longer term impacts, as global perceptions of the Strait as a dependable conduit for oil begin to change. The challenge for Gulf and Middle Eastern producers will be that there may be more capital expenditure on other regions, especially in the Americas and also in Africa, as the global concern for energy security and diversity of suppliers justifies new exploration and production.
Gulf producers are not passive in this transition. Their strategy is sophisticated and multi-track. First, they are moving aggressively down the value chain: SABIC is pivoting into advanced polymers and specialty chemicals; ADNOC’s Ruwais hub integrates petrochemicals, hydrogen, and carbon capture; and QatarEnergy is framing LNG exports increasingly around low-carbon and hydrogen derivatives. Second, they are locking in Asian demand as their primary market, deepening refinery and petrochemical investments (and in the post-war context, more oil storage) across the Indo-Pacific, where consumption growth is concentrated. Third, their ultra-low extraction costs—Aramco produces at roughly $3–5/barrel—will give them a structural advantage over higher-cost producers, which will find themselves obliged to drastically cut or even cease production. Under the IEA’s current policies scenario, OPEC+ production in 2050 is projected to be 15 percent higher than at any point in history. How OPEC+ maintains cohesion, however, is more uncertain. The UAE’s exit from OPEC in May 2026 set a precedent for regional producers eager to invest now to increase production and reach the market while demand and prices are firm. They are bolstering domestic renewables not for climate reasons, but to displace crude used domestically for power and to free up more barrels for export.
The current geopolitical situation may also have a longer-term impact on oil demand by accelerating renewable energy use, especially in the form of electric vehicles. Current geopolitical developments are sending mixed signals for the pace of the energy transition. Trade barriers and rising protectionism increase the risk of global economic slowdown, which in turn reduces hydrocarbon consumption and makes capital investment in both clean and fossil fuel energy sources more difficult and expensive. Conflict and growing nationalist politics heighten energy security risk, incentivizing countries toward domestically produced fossil fuels and renewables over imported energy. Meanwhile, China’s export orientation means that the country will continue directing surplus clean tech products—solar panels, batteries, and EVs—toward developing economies in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. China’s share of clean-tech exports to emerging economies has risen from 23 percent to 31 percent since 2022, according to a study by Bloomberg NEF.1
The net result is likely a bifurcated transition: slower in the United States and trade-war-affected economies, but faster across much of Asia and Europe. Middle East producers, with unmatched cost structures and a deliberate pivot toward petrochemicals and Asian markets, are positioning themselves to be the last hydrocarbons producers—the survivors of a decades-long shakeout among global producers. The real risk they face is not near-term demand collapse, but a 2040s world where EVs dominate transport, while petrochemicals become the final major-use case for crude. Global demand for oil is strongest now in road transport; as that demand declines, there is likely to be resilient demand in the realm of petrochemicals, manufacturing and construction, and aviation and shipping.
