Hydrocarbon Importers Must Focus on Improving Labor ProductivityThe main challenge middle-income hydrocarbon importers face is different from that of the oil exporting countries, even though it is related to hydrocarbons. While these countries would benefit directly from lower oil and gas prices, there are indirect ways in which the decline in hydrocarbon revenues in the region harms them. In particular, middle-income hydrocarbon importers depend heavily on remittances and capital flows from the GCC states, both of which will decline with a waning of hydrocarbon revenues (see figure 7). This is especially true as GCC countries are increasingly focused on hiring more nationals and are “nationalizing” an increased share of jobs for that purpose.8 Moreover, they are directing most capital toward domestic investment. Except in Morocco, Tunisia, and Jordan the remittances of oil- and gas-importing countries are larger than revenues derived from manufacturing exports. Given the lack of resources in these countries, the overarching goal should be to improve labor productivity by improving the efficiency of their economies.Progress on economic diversification and performance will depend on keeping up with changes in the world. The global economy has been transformed profoundly in the past decade. Three main developments are worth noting: the rapid evolution of high tech and artificial intelligence (AI); the reconfiguration of globalization, with geopolitical divergences between the United States and China leading to a regionalization of strategic value chains; and the pressing challenge of adapting to the effects of global warming and beginning the green transition in production processes. It is more difficult for the middle-income countries to keep pace with such transformations when compared to high-income countries. However, middle-income countries do offer valuable new opportunities that can fuel growth.Global production structures are being reshaped by technological advances—principally AI technology and robotization. Digital transformation, which shifts value creation from capital to knowledge, presents an opportunity to improve labor productivity and create well-paying jobs, especially in services. It is also an important instrument for the modernization of state services. However, policies are needed to avoid digital divides and job polarization.9 While there has been a major increase in investment in AI and digitization in high-income countries in recent years, it is still early days for the middle-income countries of the MENA region. Having invested in digital infrastructure—the “hard” side—the middle-income countries have experienced strong growth in mobile and fixed broadband subscriptions and mobile data consumption.10 At this stage, however, low skill levels are holding these countries back, and policies to ensure AI creates rather than destroys jobs are in their infancy.After decades of hyper-globalization, global trade is at a turning point. There is an ongoing trend to relocalize production closer to consumption. Doing so offsets rising geostrategic risks by situating production in nearby countries with which one enjoys friendlier ties. Moreover, the implementation of green policies in Europe involves taxing goods produced in countries with low environmental standards (the so-called Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)), thereby increasing incentives in the MENA region to adopt greener production techniques.11 The preference for producing in countries closer to Europe and the GCC can benefit the region’s middle-income countries, providing advantages for their manufacturing sectors. In this global reshuffling of production, these middle-income countries can build on their young populations, geographical position, and cultural assets. Promising sectors of activity include services in high-tech areas, as well as high-value agriculture and agribusiness.There is a tension between diversification and trade policies, which requires careful calibration of both types of strategies. Diversification policies often rely on selective protection mechanisms, subsidies, local content requirements, public procurement preferences, and strategic support for emerging sectors. This creates a paradox. Greater integration into global and regional markets is indispensable for attracting investment, accessing technology, integrating value chains, and developing export-oriented productive sectors; however, excessive or poorly sequenced trade liberalization only accelerates deindustrialization. In several countries in the region, trade openness has stimulated import growth much more quickly than export diversification, contributing to external imbalances and reinforcing rent-dependent consumption patterns rather than stimulating productive transformation.The issue is not whether openness is desirable or not, but rather how to sequence integration in a way that supports productive transformation instead of undermining it. Greater economic integration within the MENA region itself can potentially create larger protected transitional spaces capable of supporting value chains, industrial complementarities, and economies of scale before full exposure to global competition. Yet political fragmentation and divergent national strategies continue to limit such possibilities. In this context, trade agreements should not be viewed merely as commercial instruments, but as strategic political economy tools capable of either facilitating or constraining the region’s planned long-term diversification.Trade agreements should not be viewed merely as commercial instruments, but as strategic political economy tools capable of either facilitating or constraining the region’s planned long-term diversification.Climate change, a major factor affecting the region, constitutes a further complication. The MENA region is highly vulnerable to climate change through rising temperatures and sea levels, precipitation variability, desertification, and increased freshwater scarcity. Middle-income countries in the region require massive investments to adapt to global warming in ways that avert lower growth and negative distributional effects. Yet specific policies have been limited so far. One reason is that adaptation is costly, even if it is far more costly to do nothing. Given the potential public good of such projects, they need to be funded and undertaken by the state. Raising the funds needed requires improved governance. However, the region’s middle-income countries also have large potential in renewable energy and, more generally, in growing their “green economy.” Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, and Tunisia have started innovating in this sector, operating large solar farms and transforming solar energy into hydrogen.12 Countries that are geographically close to Europe will increasingly be able to export renewable energy to the continent, such as electricity and hydrogen. Moreover, while carbon border adjustment mechanisms such as CBAM can be challenging for traditional exporters, MENA countries can leverage their plentiful sunshine to develop products made with renewable energy that can enter Europe customs-free, a vital comparative advantage in the green transition.Diversification and Efficiency Trajectories: Performance, Challenges, and the Path Forward Based on recent economic performance, we can group the countries of the MENA region into two categories—high-income countries, made up of the GCC countries, and middle-income countries, which we can further subdivide into oil exporters and oil importers. High- and middle-income oil exporters depend directly on oil and gas revenues, whereas middle-income oil importers rely indirectly on oil and gas revenues, mainly through remittances and capital flows from the GCC states. The impetus to engage in diversification is more salient among hydrocarbon exporters, while the incentive to become more efficient is more relevant among hydrocarbon importers.For some time now, high-income oil-exporting countries have been investing a large portion of their oil and gas revenues in diversifying their economies and improving productivity. There have been early successes, while the challenges ahead have become clearer. Innovations in the production landscape will require industrial policies that incentivize innovation as well as massive investments, in order to create new value chains that are globally competitive. Resources are not the main constraints. The principal challenge is to ensure that checks and balances and feedback mechanisms are in place to avoid bad bets that end up as white elephants.The middle-income countries have been unable to build up their resilience to shocks and improve labor productivity. These fragilities have been exacerbated by social upheaval and rolling economic jolts after 2010–2011, when uprisings swept away regimes in the Middle East and North Africa that had held power for decades. Oil and gas exporters have tended mainly to consume rather than invest their revenues. Oil and gas importers have borrowed externally to smooth over shocks and to support consumption, in the process building up public debts that have become unsustainable. Both categories of countries will be affected by the reduced demand for hydrocarbons, either directly in the form of lower revenue or indirectly in the form of lower remittances and aid. Increased investment and improved labor productivity are thus crucial for both oil and gas importers and exporters.The High-Income Countries of the GCCWhile economic diversification has long been an objective in the Gulf states, it has become more essential in recent years. From 2008 to 2019, GCC countries launched ambitious economic and social reform agendas—often referred to as “visions”—which aimed to reduce the region’s dependency on oil. In 2008, Bahrain, Qatar, and the UAE emirate of Abu Dhabi were the first to launch their Vision 2030 agendas in the aftermath of the global financial and economic crash. In 2010, the UAE followed up with a unified Vision 2031 agenda for the whole country. Saudi Arabia launched its Vision 2030 in 2016, rapidly garnering significant international attention due to the size of the country’s economy and its central position in global energy markets. Kuwait’s Vision 2035 and Oman’s Vision 2040 followed in 2017 and 2019, respectively. These “visions” have in common the ambition of creating diversified and productive economies led by the private sector, through job creation in sectors that can be globally competitive. Through a variety of approaches, they have sought to improve their country’s fiscal balance, increase productive investments (including by attracting foreign direct investment), enhance government effectiveness, equip their workforces with up-to-date skills, strengthen their business environment, and transform their private sector into engines of growth.The change in the pace of reforms has accelerated in recent years. The UAE has pulled ahead of other countries. Smaller and poorer Gulf states such as Oman and Bahrain have lagged behind and face significant fiscal challenges.13 In Saudi Arabia, Vison 2030 has already ushered in the emergence of a more liberal culture, the digitization of government services, a jump in female labor-force participation, the introduction of taxes, and the reform of subsidy systems. In other areas, however, gains have remained more modest.14To develop new sectors, GCC countries are experimenting with vigorous industrial policies. In Saudi Arabia, for example, the Public Investment Fund (PIF) has played a major role in this effort by investing heavily in the productive sector—injecting around 5 percent of GDP per year. The PIF was set up to support reforms in several ways: by commercializing state-owned enterprises (SOEs), improving their productivity, and readying them for privatization; by initiating innovative projects and creating new companies that could become successful in their areas in partnership with the private sector; by investing in transformative megaprojects (NEOM, Qiddiya, the Red Sea) that create investment opportunities for the private sector; by supporting the growth of small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and encouraging the growth of fledgling firms, contributing to their financing and creating market opportunities for their operations; and by helping to shape government policies and institutions that support economic growth.However, there is still a large gap between dreams and realities. The reform efforts fall short of some of their intended objectives, most notably the creation of jobs adequate to absorb a rising cohort of educated youth, which would require turning the private sector into an engine of innovation and growth.15 In Saudi Arabia, the goal was to increase the private sector’s share in the country’s GDP from 40 percent in 2016 to 65 percent in 2030. Yet in 2025 it still stood at only 43 percent. And compared to a Saudi goal of increasing non-hydrocarbon exports to 50 percent of exports by 2030, the figure in 2025 stood at 27 percent, a minor increase from the 16 percent baseline of 2016. Non-hydrocarbon exports account for only around 10 percent of total exports in Kuwait and Qatar, 25 percent in Oman, and exceed 50 percent in the UAE and Bahrain.16 Private-sector activity in the GCC continues to rely heavily on government-funded projects and on consumption, both supported by oil and gas revenues. In Bahrain, hydrocarbons account for a small share of GDP due largely to depleted reserves, but the country continues to support economic activity indirectly through transfers and spending from neighboring countries.17 Much remains to be done to achieve meaningful diversification. Figure 8 shows how diversification in the GCC countries compares to those of other regions. The index of diversification—produced by the Bin Rashid School of Government in Dubai—measures the extent to which output, trade, and government revenue have been diversified away from oil and gas.18 All GCC states are below the global trend line. The UAE leads the GCC, followed closely by Kuwait, Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, while Qatar and Oman are laggards. The sub-indicators (not shown) suggest that most of the progress occurred in the production of non-tradable goods, followed by modest advancement in the production of tradable goods that could be exported.There are four challenges to overcome if the GCC states are to diversify their economies in a sustainable way. The first is to discover more areas in which they can be competitive internationally. The second is to conduct effective industrial policies by identifying anappropriate role for the state as investor, regulator, or planner. The third is to move beyond the temptation of state capitalism and foster an innovative private sector. The fourth is to convince economic and ruling elites to accept the growth of autonomous businesses even though these might threaten their market shares, and even their political hegemony.The first challenge, therefore, is to produce goods and services on a globally competitive basis. The production of non-tradables, mainly services, is not particularly difficult, given that domestic markets are naturally protected. The main issue is one of cost. A haircut might be cheaper if delivered by an expatriate from a poor country than by a national, but it might be more desirable for the state to insist that a national be the hairdresser, even at a higher wage, given the pressure to create jobs for nationals. Producing tradables is more challenging, since these need to be produced at a competitive cost to survive competition from abroad. The question is whether competitiveness can be improved sufficiently to make the production of tradables profitable outside obvious areas such as tourism. There are several positive developmental advantages underway, such as the fact that the hefty revenues that GCC countries earn from oil and gas allow them to finance large investments—in petrochemicals, aluminum, or fertilizers—where they have become globally competitive. Other rising sectors, such as tourism and hospitality, can benefit from relatively cheap foreign labor.There is also a geographical advantage in being situated at the intersection of large markets in the East and West, a feature that Saudi Arabia, in its Vision 2030, sees as allowing it to construct a modern, European-like industrial giant. But there are also technical constraints associated with being located in a part of the world where temperatures are high and expected to rise further. GCC states are already the world’s highest per capita consumers of oil and gas. That is how they desalinize water, air-condition homes and offices, and drive on highways in modern urban spaces largely devoid of public transportation. When one adds emissions from oil and gas production, these countries move into the top ranks of carbon-dioxide producers. On a per capita basis, Qatar is number-one globally, followed in second and third place by Bahrain and Kuwait.19The second challenge is to create industries from scratch. To establish new sectors, “horizontal” policies will not suffice. For example, launching a tourism sector requires infrastructure, hotels, new skills, museums, specialized services, and so on. In this transformation, individual firms face several market failures that may impinge on their long-term success and require public interventions, such as: imitation by competitors; a need to rely on other goods and services that are not produced yet (for example, vocational training); and the risk of losing the workers they train at great expense to competitors.As with industrial policies more generally, the question is not so much whether public action to get businesses off the ground are needed but how to implement them in ways that work.20 When a state decides which firms to subsidize in order to create state champions in new fields deemed worthy of development, there remains the risk of state failure, in particular rent-seeking, clientelism, and cronyism. This risk is even higher when resources are distributed to entrepreneurs according to loyalty rather than efficiency. In the past, Gulf states placed great emphasis on supporting their business elites—successors to the merchant elites associated with the birth of their nation. Over time, these elites came to preside over major business concerns. This led to the development of a powerful “Gulf super-bourgeoisie,”21 which includes politically connected businesses that benefit from their closeness to power. Such connections risk stifling incentives to innovate. To truly favor innovation, Gulf states will need to democratize, if not their politics then at least their markets, through greater reliance on competition.To truly favor innovation, Gulf states will need to democratize, if not their politics then at least their markets, through greater reliance on competition.The third challenge is to create an innovative productive sector. There are currently three layers of firms in the Gulf states. Sitting on top are the largest ones, which have the most capital and are the most skill-intensive. This top layer includes hydrocarbon-related industries (such as Saudi Arabia’s SABIC) as well as many of the large firms in the financial, logistics, and utilities sectors. They tend to be well-run and apply cutting-edge technologies. The second tier is made up of large private firms owned by leading families. These tend to be more labor-intensive and critically dependent on energy subsidies as well as on favorable trade and labor policies. They have traditionally dealt in public procurement and imports, expanding over time to the construction, manufacturing, banking, real estate, and service sectors. While these firms have progressed a great deal since the first oil boom, most of their activities still amount to rent recycling rather than autonomous diversification. The underlying driver of their demand remains in large part government procurement and local demand for non-tradables. When moving into more technologically complex sectors, they often do so in partnership with SOEs.There is also a third tier, one made up of SMEs. These are shops, restaurants, hotels, firms engaged in transport and construction subcontracting, all of which offer non-tradable services. This sector is characterized by strong competition, which has pushed innovation in order to survive. The difficulty here, especially as the rise of information technology has started to disrupt the corporate landscape, is to allow these firms to compete with established companies, and to refrain from unduly protecting the latter.SOEs, which the Gulf states have increasingly mobilized to advance their strategic objectives, are more pliable to the sovereign’s wishes than are private entrepreneurs. As a result, the current model, which can still evolve, seems de facto to be largely based on building state-owned national champions. This unique system of “state capitalism” has strengths, as SOEs involved in sectors such as electricity, water and sanitation, and transportation have traditionally been well-managed in most GCC countries.22 But now that the focus is on the production of all tradable goods, state capitalism increasingly runs the risk of creating industries that remain dependent on government support, as happened during the pre-1980s import-substitution era in much of the developing world.23 It has been estimated that the consolidated public sector, including sovereign wealth funds, public financial institutions, and ministries, owns more than 80 percent of stock market capitalization in the UAE, Bahrain, Oman, and Qatar, 73 percent in Saudi Arabia, and 53 percent in Kuwait.24 In economies increasingly dominated by large firms, there is little competition. Most of these firms enjoy monopoly rights or similar privileges over the extraction of resources, access to cheap energy for energy-intensive industries, access to land for mega real estate companies, and access to enormous amounts of financing. The challenge is to start SOEs on the right footing, ensure a system of governance that creates checks and balances to keep productivity and competitiveness high, and privatize companies when conditions are ripe.The fourth and most difficult challenge is political. A competitive model requires that firms succeed or fail based on performance, as opposed to their closeness to the ruler. But it is questionable whether the relatively young rulers in the Gulf countries today, focused as they are on centralizing power, would be comfortable with a strong private sector, which could support opposition political forces in the future. In the past, Gulf businesses’ strong dependence on the state allowed the political leadership to maintain a degree of control over a capitalist class that might otherwise have challenged its power. As state-distributed support weakens, however, so too does this control. Previously, the GCC’s wealthy ruling elites secured themselves and consolidated power without resorting to the high levels of repression found in middle-income countries. The question now is whether the hydrocarbon shock tied to the conflict with Iran will push these countries toward more economic inclusion or toward a more exclusionary type of political settlement.25
Box 2. Oman and Bahrain: Early Diversifiers by Necessity
Kristin Diwan
The hydrocarbons that elevated the Gulf region to great wealth and global prominence are not evenly distributed. Among the six members of the Gulf Cooperation Council, Bahrain and Oman have significantly fewer oil and gas reserves. Consequently, their governments were forced by necessity to pursue diversification. The two countries’ experiences of “early” diversification differed, however, due to the timing of state-building and economic development trajectories in each. These differing experiences are revealing and illustrate distinct periods of Gulf global economic integration as well as the impact on Gulf states of global finance and technological change.
An Early Diversifier and a Late Developer
Bahrain was the first state to discover oil and the first state, effectively, to run out of it. Oil production began on the island in 1932, with commercial exports beginning shortly thereafter. Importantly, the first oil refinery was built in 1936, launching the expansion into refined product and expanding Bahrain’s hydrocarbon industry. Yet by the 1970s, when other Gulf states began exporting and profiting from oil with vastly more significant returns, Bahrain’s oil production had already peaked. Since then, Bahrain has been dependent on oil that is contributed to its refinery by Saudi Arabia.
Bahrain’s diversification from oil, then, began in earnest in the 1970s. Aluminum Bahrain (Alba) began production in 1971, establishing Bahrain as one of the largest exporters of aluminum globally. The country’s move into financial services was aided by the decline of Beirut as a financial hub due to the Lebanese Civil War; this added to Manama’s economic portfolio in offshore banking, tourism, and other businesses predominantly oriented toward Saudi Arabia.
Like Bahrain, Oman had fewer hydrocarbon resources than its neighbors. But unlike Bahrain, Oman was hindered by the inherent conservatism of its early ruler, Sultan Said bin Taimur, and thus developed those resources relatively late. Oil-fueled development had to wait until Sultan Said’s overthrow by his son, Qaboos bin Said, in 1970, and began in earnest only in the 1980s. Oman did not pursue economic diversification until 1995, when it launched Vision 2020—which focused on heavy manufacturing and petrochemicals based in Oman’s ports. Under Oman’s current ruler, Sultan Haitham bin Tariq, a push for greater structural reform and fiscal discipline has begun attracting more foreign investment, thereby allowing for the expansion of tourism and new industries, notably renewable energy and green hydrogen.
Social Contracts: Similarities and Distinctions
Bahrain’s early diversification into industry introduced the country to labor politics. The concentration of workers in Alba and the Bahrain Petroleum Company, for example, led to unionization. With Bahrain’s majority-Shiite population suffering from a degree of state exclusion, its members were pushed into the private sector in higher numbers. This has contributed to a familiar pattern of periodic social unrest in Bahrain, at times with class characteristics and at other times marked by a more religious-sectarian mobilization.   
Following a Marxist insurgency in the 1960s–1970s, political unrest in Oman began to diminish. In the 2000s, there was a focus on preparing state-owned sectors and parastatals for privatization. This, along with Oman’s historic reliance on a foreign-born business class, has fed periodic populist discontent and labor demonstrations, particularly in the port town of Sohar.
Resilience and the Post–Iran War Future
Oman’s late development meant that it and Bahrain experienced diversification and global integration at different periods and with differing technologies. There are advantages to Oman’s late diversification, such as the fact that the country is now in a position to benefit from industries better suited to the current era of green energy transition and transport logistics. In contrast, Manama has lost some of its earlier advantages, surrendering to Dubai its leading position in finance, particularly in the Islamic sector. With Saudi Arabia’s political opening, some of Bahrain’s advantages as an offshore market are also at risk.
The Iran war of 2026 has amplified these vulnerabilities. Oman’s geographic location in the Indian Ocean provides advantages unavailable to Bahrain, which is trapped north of the Strait of Hormuz. Politically, Oman has remained open to Iran as well as to China. Bahrain, in turn, views Iran as an existential threat. This has contributed to Manama’s dependence on Saudi Arabia, and more recently on fellow Abraham Accord countries the United Arab Emirates and Israel. Moving forward, Bahrain will require support from its Gulf partners, while Oman may benefit from new transport and energy logistics that enable it to skirt Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz.
The Middle-Income CountriesMiddle income countries in the Middle East and North Africa, both oil and gas exporters and importers, seem stuck in what has been called the middle-income trap.26 The advantages that propel high growth in poor countries during their early development phases—low labor costs and the adoption of basic technologies—disappear when they reach middle-income levels. Finding new and sustainable sources of growth depends on society’s ability to develop country-specific solutions to complex problems, such as improving resilience to shocks without upsetting social or macroeconomic balances, while also upgrading productivity by improving the quality of education, developing and delivering industrial policies, and embedding checks and balances in governance to improve system performance.Finding new and sustainable sources of growth depends on society’s ability to develop country-specific solutions to complex problems. For many of the middle-income countries in the MENA region, the decade after the uprisings that began in 2010–2011 was a period of economic stagnation and decay. As indicated in figure 9, current growth rates are the lowest since the 1960s for oil and gas importers, even worse than during the lost decade of the 1980s. Most regimes spent the decade of 2010–2020 trying to assert or reassert authority, but were often unable to deal with internal turmoil and external shocks. State-business relations were characterized by distrust, leading to record low investment levels. Relations between state and society also deteriorated as social mobility regressed, underemployment increased, and public services deteriorated. Several countries seemed unable to confront major new challenges such as technological change, deglobalization, and climate change.Two main factors have prevented middle-income countries from growing. The first is an inability to absorb economic shocks without generating costly macroeconomic imbalances that weaken political settlements by creating social dissatisfaction and slowing private-sector growth. The second is the collapse of labor productivity. The ability to absorb shocks is related to both the availability of counter-cyclical external finance and the political elites’ capacity to forge coalitions that share the costs of adjustment fairly. In the tight global capital markets after 2023, external financing became scarce and the GCC was too concerned with its own development challenges to provide as wide a financial safety net as in the past.27 And following the uprisings of a decade earlier, the choice of political elites to restrict freedom of association and expression weakened states’ ability to encourage dialogue that could have helped forge reformist alliances.As in other developing countries, the middle-income countries of the MENA region were badly affected by a series of major negative external shocks in the years after 2019. The first was the COVID-19 pandemic, during which fiscal deficits grew in response to measures designed to ease the pandemic’s effects on households and firms. Then, Russia’s war on Ukraine raised fuel prices, harming oil and gas importers in 2022. After global capital markets tightened in 2023 following the attempts of rich countries to curb inflation through interest rate hikes, middle-income countries were cut off from international financial markets, exacerbating their financial constraints. Israel’s war in Gaza, which began that year, devastated the Palestinian economy while also disrupting that of Israel itself, as well as those of Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria. Earlier conflicts in Libya, Syria, and Yemen undermined not just the economies of these countries but also those of their neighbors. Most recently, the Iran war has raised oil prices substantially, weakening the external accounts of countries in the region and exacerbating financial difficulties. These developments came on the heels of a decade of expansionary fiscal and monetary policies in Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, and Tunisia. Most of the regimes in the region, battered by the political waves generated by the uprisings after 2010–2011, overused expansionary policies to buy social stability. This was financed largely through external debt, as capital markets were flush with cheap liquidity following the expansionary monetary policies of Western countries after the global financial crisis of 2008. But as external finance dried out, deficits grew because of the need to service foreign debt, and at the same time they increasingly had to be financed domestically, crowding out investment in the private sector, hurting growth.28Rising macroeconomic imbalances and political risk have taken a toll on national investment efforts (see figure 10). The average total investment in oil importing and exporting middle-income countries has fallen since 2020. The performance of total investment was a combination of two factors—a fall in public investment and a lack of growth in private investment. Private-sector performance was especially disappointing in Egypt, where private investment remained around 10 percent of GDP in the first decade of the century, and in Morocco, where it was only slightly higher, 11 percent of GDP, while in Jordan it reached around 20 percent of GDP. The middle-income oil exporters benefited from relatively elevated oil and gas prices, which created an opportunity to invest in diversification. But while their investment rate was a bit higher than oil and gas importers, this represented a missed opportunity, as their additional revenues were largely spent on security and consumption.A second factor that has prevented middle-income countries from growing is that labor productivity, which rose during the period of economic reforms between 1990 and 2010, fell after 2010. Market liberalization, though unbalanced, allowed for improvements in efficiency in the 1990s and the first decade of the century. During this period, productivity also improved in the sprawling private sectors of states in the MENA region, and in privatized agricultural cooperatives. Large state-owned enterprises producing negative value added were dismantled. Over time, labor and capital found better opportunities in small firms and even in the informal sector. But liberalization did not create a dynamic formal private sector. The spread of politically connected crony capitalists in most economies of the region limited the scope of efficiency gains.29 After 2011, macro instability, namely unsustainable deficits, as well as political instability, deterred not only private activity but also innovation. These trends are apparent in figure 11, where the growth of total factor productivity (TFP), which measures improvements in labor productivity, and which had risen during the adjustment period, fell to zero or even negative numbers in all parts of the MENA region after 2011. By comparison, economic growth in East and South Asia showed TFP growth of about 2 percent per year.30 For middle-income countries, the current situation is as challenging as the crisis period of the 1980s, when the state-led inward growth model collapsed. That period led to major economic reforms, including economic liberalization, the rollback of the state, and a strengthening of the private sector.31 This time, the challenge is just as significant, but different: Instead of creating markets, the real question is how to make markets work. It is also how to address the new challenges of climate adaptation, digitalization, trade regionalization, and AI. Different countries are responding differently. Lebanon has not started adjusting to the strains of its financial crisis.32 Egypt and Jordan have chosen to balance their books by imposing heavy austerity measures.33 Tunisia is favoring consumption over investment. Such measures have combined to reduce investment to historically low levels. Austerity has also increased the risks of social instability (discussed in the next section).Among the middle-income countries of the MENA, only Morocco is actively attempting to push the technology frontier and move into higher labor-productivity sectors. Morocco’s ability to achieve more sectoral upgrading than other middle-income oil and gas importers has been driven by an active and relatively successful industrial policy, a rarity in the region.34 The establishment of industrial zones and export-driven strategies has attracted significant foreign direct investment, making Morocco a manufacturing hub that benefits from its proximity to European markets. There has been remarkable growth in its automotive industry, with the kingdom becoming Africa’s largest car exporter. Morocco’s aerospace sector has, similarly, benefited from partnerships with global players. FDI has poured into renewable energy, taking advantage of an attractive regulatory regime.35 As in other countries, FDI-led industrialization raises the question of shallow versus deep integration—that is, whether spillovers and local linkages are strong enough to improve the domestic content of global value chains over time. In both the automotive and aerospace sectors, the current challenges are to increase the share of local content and foster innovation. Morocco’s national phosphate company, the OCP Group (formerly Office Chérifien des Phosphates), has also pursued an ambitious industrial-upgrading strategy. These strides coexist, however, with entrenched challenges that prevent a rapid rise in productivity. High levels of investment have powered infrastructure expansion and some industrialization, but economic growth remains low and fluctuating. Social challenges, including high youth unemployment, limited female workforce participation, high income and regional disparities, and lingering poverty, all underscore the need for a more inclusive development framework.The twin constraints of stabilization and technological upgrading has played out differently across hydrocarbon importers and exporters, particularly after the breakout of the Arab uprisings in 2010–2011. The middle-income oil and gas importers suffered most from economic instability because of relatively high hydrocarbon prices as well as the tightening of the global financial market on which they depended for external loans. Middle-income hydrocarbon exporters, on the other hand, had access to relatively high oil and gas revenues, which helped create a more stable macro-environment. Yet the leaderships’ distrust of the private sector in these countries, and their very high reliance on loyal politically connected firms to dominate markets, have meant that private-sector development remained marginal at best. Unlike their rich GCC neighbors, the middle-income oil exporters have not progressed on economic diversification.The difficulties that middle-income countries have faced are quite distinct from those that high-income countries face, as the former are grappling with much higher levels of vulnerability, even as they have less access to investable resources. The four key challenges for middle-income countries in attempting to increase investment and labor productivity are building buffers and resilience to avoid overreactions to shock; mobilizing domestic savings and increasing labor force participation; encouraging the spread of innovation, which requires dynamic competitive pressures; and, as with high-income countries, developing a political will to enact reform.The first objective, building up the resilience of economies and societies, should be a priority, given the prevalence of shocks in the Middle East and North Africa as well as globally. At the macroeconomic level, this requires more care in managing external capital flows as well as more effort to attract productive FDI to supplement domestic savings. At the level of households, social protection needs to be beefed up to ensure that shocks do not create poverty traps that delay development through intergenerational effects. Universal subsidies need to be reformed because they are fiscally expensive (taking up a large share of public expenditures in most countries), economically inefficient (they foster over-consumption), and unfair socially (they benefit the rich more than the poor). Targeted social safety nets, which are geared toward the poor, resolve many of these problems.36 Improvements are necessary to increase coverage, improve targeting, expand transparency, and fight clientelism and corruption. They need to be supplemented by more generous support for social security—pensions, health insurance, and education for all.A second aim, given the scarcity of resources, is to mobilize savings and labor participation. Low economic dynamism and a lack of opportunities have led to the demobilization of societies, whereby the countries of the MENA region have low saving rates and low labor force participation. These trends have to be reversed to support a rising growth path that can be sustained over time. In most middle-income countries in the region, national saving rates are below 10 percent of GDP, less than a third of the average in middle-income countries globally.37 Low national savings are due to large public deficits but also reflect low corporate and household savings. At a time when foreign resources have become scarce, self-help becomes a necessity.Tax revenues are also low in most MENA countries. National efforts must broaden the tax base and make it more progressive. Part of the problem is related to the pervasiveness of informality. Renewed efforts to provide social security for all, as is currently being considered in Morocco, would raise both tax revenues and domestic savings. The scarcity of good jobs has led many people to withdraw from the labor force: average male labor force participation in middle-income countries of the MENA region hovers around 70 percent, which is 5 percentage points below the global average.38 Even worse, this rate is 17.5 percent for women, far below the global average of 50 percent.39 Low female participation is due not only to patriarchal social orders, which are slow to change, but also to the scarcity of jobs. In more dynamic economies, a rise in female labor force participation would allow three important evolutions, namely personal empowerment and emancipation, which leads to improved child education and lower fertility; higher household incomes, which can sustain the middle class in the face of declining wages; and higher economic growth, including through the development of new sectors such as childcare and care for the elderly, as well as other household services.A third challenge is to promote innovation—doing more with less. This requires a number of prerequisites. Most prominent among them, however, is the need to ensure a level playing field in terms of competition. More than elsewhere, autocratic regimes in the MENA region have sought to dominate the private sector and protect their allies rather than allow the emergence of a genuinely autonomous entrepreneurial ecosystem. By forsaking the benefits of creative destruction, whereby low-productivity firms are allowed to go out of business and make room for more efficient firms, production factors are channeled to firms that are loyal rather than to those that can employ them most productively. Maintaining privileges encourages protectionism, which prevents importing more advanced technology. It also misuses production factors and misallocates state resources. And it reduces the dynamism of economies by preventing competition, which is the main driver of innovation. As a result, industrial sectors around the region have become largely devoid of the drive needed to climb the technology ladder, let alone participate in global value chains.Such dynamics can be observed across several GCC countries, but this phenomenon is especially costly in the middle-income countries. Algeria illustrates the dilemma clearly, as diversification policies continue to rely heavily on public-sector structures despite repeated calls for greater private-sector dynamism.40 Egypt presents a variation on the same phenomenon through the growing centrality of the military-industrial complex within large segments of the economy.41 In Libya, fragmented state structures and rent distribution mechanisms continue to constrain the emergence of productive entrepreneurial dynamics.42 Iraq has become more fragmented politically, trapped in clientelistic and crony relations that do not favor private-sector activity and productivity gains.43 Tunisia may represent another worrying trajectory. After having historically developed one of the region’s most significant private industrial bases, the country now appears to be gradually drifting toward a model characterized by growing state intervention, institutional uncertainty, and the progressive weakening of productive private actors.44Diversification is not only about sectors or investment volumes. It is also about the distribution of economic power, the autonomy of productive actors, and the institutional environment within which entrepreneurship evolves.Finally, a fourth objective is to muster the political will to gamble on development. A growth compact requires political involvement and courage, ingredients that have been missing in the past. For too long, structural reforms have been off the table. Ultimately, diversification is not only about sectors or investment volumes. It is also about the distribution of economic power, the autonomy of productive actors, and the institutional environment within which entrepreneurship evolves. But fragile political regimes have feared the reaction of those losing out in the short term, and have not managed to mobilize majorities that stand to gain in the long term. Important constituencies—unionized labor, economic elites, consumers—need to be convinced to take short term-losses, against a promise of larger long-term gains. In doing so, these constituencies would be betting that political and social coordination improve markedly compared to poor past performances. Successful reform plans need to be based on a broadly accepted narrative of renewal and progress, with the power to mobilize politicians, social activists, innovators, and entrepreneurs. This requires ameliorations in the freedom of organization and expression, which is critical to mobilizing the youth and middle classes.Social Contracts Under Pressure: Reform Dilemmas and the Politics of DiversificationAcross the Middle East and North Africa, state-society arrangements that have historically combined distribution, patronage, coercion, symbolic legitimation, and varying degrees of political acquiescence are under mounting strain. The generation now entering the labor market is better educated than its predecessors, harbors higher aspirations, and has grown up with social media and exposure to global living standards. Yet it also faces higher unemployment, deteriorating public services, and more precarious labor markets. This mismatch between educational investment and economic opportunity is the product of structural vulnerabilities compounded by reform paths that have been incomplete, deferred, or insufficiently deep to alter underlying dynamics in countries, thereby straining social contracts across the region.However, the nature of that tension varies across the GCC countries, middle-income hydrocarbon exporters, and middle-income hydrocarbon importers, because each category of countries rests on a fundamentally different distributional bargain. In the GCC, the classic rentier bargain, in which hydrocarbon wealth was exchanged for political acquiescence, is being quietly restructured through labor nationalization policies, subsidy cuts, and the introduction of taxation. Citizens are being asked to compete in a market economy while the state withdraws guarantees it once provided, thereby generating grievances that find few formal outlets. This situation risks making uncertain transitions even more challenging.In middle-income hydrocarbon exporting countries, such as Algeria, Iraq, and Libya, the social contract is based on distributing rents for consumption rather than channeling them toward productive diversification.45 However, though moderate oil and gas revenues are sufficient to sustain narrow patronage networks and security apparatuses, they are insufficient to finance mass consumption and command broad legitimacy. The result is an exclusionary political settlement in which access to public resources results from loyalty rather than productivity, while jobs for youth are scarce, unemployment is high, and the younger generation has been frustrated and restless for decades. In middle-income oil importing nations, such as Egypt and Jordan, the social contract has rested not on domestic resource rents but on geopolitical rents—financial windfalls to which governments have access as a result of their geographical location and security cooperation or alignment, mainly with the United States. This external pillar has been eroding, leaving governments with shrinking fiscal space, mounting debts, and rising social tensions. What unites all three groups is a common dilemma: the reforms required to build productive, diversified economies are politically costly in the short term, generating immediate losers among both regime-linked elites and ordinary households, while the benefits accrue slowly and in a dispersed manner. But inaction is economically unsustainable in the medium to long term. Faced with this situation, regimes across all three country groups have reached for the same tools: the centralization of power and intensification of repression, albeit for different purposes. GCC states have done so while pursuing reform, mainly to control the social repercussions. This has produced transitions that are incomplete and that risk undermining the very conditions meaningful diversification requires. Because they have less fiscal space and weaker state capacity than the GCC countries, both middle-income hydrocarbon exporters and most middle-income hydrocarbon importers have largely employed the same instruments of control, but not to manage reform so much as to avoid it. Essentially, they have deferred their transition toward productive, diversified economies while deepening fiscal vulnerability. In the middle-income countries, the political methods adopted to navigate the short-term costs of the reform dilemma are actually eroding the foundations of durable reform.The questions politicians face in all countries are complex. They have to propose credible reforms that generate support from reform coalitions, create mechanisms to compensate losers and bring them into the fold, and introduce checks and balances to incorporate lessons learned and avoid costly mistakes. Finally, they also have to allow for the voicing of dissatisfaction to avoid the type of explosions of anger that were common during the past decade. Underlying all of this is a deeper imperative, namely constructing new foundations of legitimacy rooted in productivity, inclusion, and credible governance. Between Two Pacts: The GCC’s Unfinished Social ContractThe experiences of young GCC nationals today diverge sharply from those of their parents, reflecting a fundamental reconfiguration of the social contracts in GCC states. The classic rentier bargain rested on the redistribution of hydrocarbon wealth to citizens in exchange for limiting their political participation. In practice, this meant guaranteed public-sector employment at wages and benefits substantially exceeding those of the private sector. Public employment percentages for nationals reached around 90 percent in some states.46 The fiscal weight of this arrangement was considerable: In 2021, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimated that public-sector wage bills were roughly 9 to 10 percent of GDP in Bahrain, Qatar, and Oman, and substantially higher in Saudi Arabia at nearly 16 percent, and in Kuwait at about 19.5 percent.47 While nationals dominated the public sector, the private sector was overwhelmingly staffed by expatriates, who in countries such as the UAE and Qatar constituted more than 90 percent of the private workforce.48 Citizens, meanwhile, paid no income tax and benefited from heavily subsidized energy, utilities, and staple goods, enabling a low cost of living that formed a cornerstone of the social pact.Economic diversification has gradually reshaped the rentier contract into a more productive arrangement, one in which citizens are expected to participate in and contribute to a diversified economy, rather than simply receive the proceeds of oil wealth. This transition, however, has not been matched by a comparable adjustment in the material conditions or expectations the rentier era created among citizens. There is a structural tension at the heart of the GCC’s diversification projects. Essentially, the old contracts not only provided jobs and subsidies; they also shaped an entire intergenerational framework of anticipation of what the state owed its citizens and what constituted a decent livelihood. Yet diversification has dismantled the material foundations of that framework more quickly than it has built new ones, leaving a generation caught between inherited expectations and a reality that no longer matches those expectations. The public employment guarantee, the most tangible expression of the rentier contract, has been progressively reduced over the past decade, as nationalization policies have pushed citizens into private-sector roles.49 In hydrocarbon-exporting states with shrinking per capita revenues, this has led to a generation of young nationals employed in the private sector that is earning wages often significantly lower than what public employment once offered (see figure 12).50 Meanwhile, high-skilled, well-compensated positions remain largely occupied by expatriates.51This wage compression has coincided with mounting cost-of-living pressures that have further eroded the material foundations of the old bargain. Subsidy cuts implemented across the GCC countries from the second decade of the century onward have driven up the price of fuel, utilities, services, and housing.52 Compounding the difficulty of the new situation for citizens, GCC governments have pursued revenue diversification through taxation. Value-added taxes have been introduced by four of the six GCC member states—typically at 5 percent, rising to 10 percent in Bahrain and 15 percent in Saudi Arabia—alongside new corporate tax frameworks, particularly in the UAE.53 By 2023, non-oil tax revenues ranged from 1 percent of GDP in Kuwait to 9 percent in Saudi Arabia.54 The result is a cost-of-living environment very different from the one in which the previous generation lived.Female labor force participation has risen across the GCC countries in recent years, driven in part by genuine gains in educational attainment and social liberalization, but also by the simple reality that a single private-sector salary cannot sustain a household.One consequence of all this is the growing normalization of dual-income households in parts of the GCC, a shift that is not solely a reflection of changing social attitudes, but also of economic necessity.55 Female labor force participation has risen across the GCC countries in recent years, driven in part by genuine gains in educational attainment and social liberalization, but also by the simple reality that a single private-sector salary cannot sustain a household. Even with two incomes, many young couples struggle to acquire property or finance a wedding—milestones whose costs have risen sharply while the wages available to nationals have not kept pace.Youth unemployment among nationals has emerged as a further source of contention. What was historically a near non-issue has become increasingly acute in a context of segmented labor markets and a persistent preference for public-sector work. Many young nationals continue to expect from the private sector the security and compensation that their parents received from the state, a mismatch that inflates reservation wages, or the minimum wage deemed sufficient to accept a job offer.In fact, the situation has led to rising grievances in the Gulf, alongside a growing gap between nationals who have successfully navigated the new, more productive pact and those left behind by it. This has been driven by rising inequality due to wage dispersion—the wage gap between nationals in high-paying, high-skilled jobs and those in low-paying jobs—and unequal access to high-skilled employment within societies.56 Taken together, these dynamics are creating strains in the social and political sustainability of the GCC’s diversification strategies.

The traditional social contract in the GCC is centrally based on government employment: Since at least the 1973 oil boom, most male GCC citizens have come to expect to sooner or later land a secure and reasonably well-paid government job.
While there are other ways in which GCC governments share wealth with their citizens—including energy subsidies, free education, free healthcare, direct welfare payments, and housing support—government employment is by far the largest channel of wealth distribution. This has resulted in both bureaucratic bloat and unusually high wage spending, reaching up to 50 percent of total government expenditure in some cases.
This old social contract is gradually coming apart,1 however. In Bahrain, Oman, and Saudi Arabia, countries with relatively lower oil income per capita, young citizens have lost access to the de facto government job guarantee that their parents enjoyed. At the same time, they are faring badly in private labor markets due to acute competition with large numbers of low-wage migrants. The UAE, Qatar, and Kuwait have relatively larger fiscal resources to maintain government employment, but are likely to face similar challenges in the long run.
Due to ongoing fiscal deficits, wage spending in lower-rent Gulf countries has plateaued during the last decade. As working-age citizen populations continue to grow, the freeze in public employment means that new job market entrants have only a small chance of getting a government job. This has created a new constituency of citizens who are labor market outsiders and have to make do in the private sector.
Finding good private employment is difficult, however, for a number of reasons. First, and most important, citizens in the low- to mid-skilled segments of the market face unusually harsh competition with low-cost migrant labor due to GCC economies’ large-scale reliance on foreign workers from the Global South with very low wage expectations. The state-employed middle class and the private sector benefit from this, but citizen labor-market outsiders are paying a steep price for it, as wages outside of the small high-skilled market segment are low. Second, there is limited government support for citizens in the private sector. While there are minimum wages for citizens and national employment quotas for private firms, these do little to provide quality employment or middle-class wages (if anything, minimum wages make citizens less competitive vis-à-vis foreigners who are not subject to such rules). There is good evidence that the presence of growing outsider strata has shaped politics across the GCC during the past two decades.2 The majority of public demonstrations across the region have been economically motivated. Key demands of demonstrators have typically included the provision of government jobs as well as more government support to provide better-paying private sector jobs and social security provision equivalent to that in the public sector. These are clearly outsider concerns. Even the Bahrain uprising in 2011, while primarily aiming at regime change, drew on a long tradition of protest by un- and underemployed young citizens.3
The Saudi leadership has generated substantial goodwill among young Saudis through liberalizing social reforms that have accompanied Mohammed bin Salman’s austerity measures. Yet social discontent could reemerge as members of the Vision 2030 generation grow older and want to start families and acquire property, undertakings that will prove difficult if private sector wages for labor market “outsiders” do not rise.

Such tensions are unfolding against the backdrop of a precarious dual wager made by most GCC governments.57 The first wager is economic, and holds that diversification can generate enough well-paying private-sector jobs to replace the economic security the state once provided directly. Yet building globally competitive industries, persuading a population accustomed to wealth distribution to compete in a market economy, and replacing oil revenues with export-driven growth represent major challenges, especially in countries with lower hydrocarbon rents per capita such as Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, and Bahrain. The second wager, this one sociopolitical in nature, is that diversification can happen quickly and broadly enough to keep the social contract from unraveling under the pressures it faces. These two wagers are mutually dependent in that a faltering economy negatively affects a country’s political situation, while a dissatisfied or restive population undermines the conditions necessary for economic success.58Yet there is a deeper political dilemma at the heart of the diversification project. A productive economy requires a genuinely competitive private sector insulated from political interference. But if the private sector becomes autonomous enough, it could become a source of independent power that threatens the stability and security of GCC regimes accustomed to controlling their business elites by keeping them dependent on state patronage. Indeed, the very dynamism that diversification demands is also what rulers have historically had reason to fear and avoid. It is precisely to address such fears that most regimes in the GCC have concentrated power and constructed new narratives legitimizing their authority. Each of these steps has its own logic as a tool of social engineering and population management. Yet taken together, they may actually compound rather than resolve the underlying dilemma. And, in doing so, they could gradually undermine the very conditions on which the economic wager depends.Over the past decade, most GCC states have seen a significant concentration of decisionmaking authority in the hands of a single leader. The old model of dynastic rule, in which power was distributed across different branches of ruling families, has given way to more centralized personal rule, most visibly under Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Saudi Arabia and Mohammed bin Zayed in the UAE. This has extended into the economic sphere, with the appointment of senior royals to lead major state-owned enterprises, sovereign wealth funds, and economic ministries, reflecting the degree to which centralized political control has infiltrated economic governance. Such consolidation has gone hand-in-hand with the marginalization of established business elites in most GCC states. Such elites, which once had some degree of access and influence, now largely operate at the state’s discretion, with little institutional voice in economic decisionmaking and effectively none in political life.59When decisionmaking is reduced to a small circle of people shielded from scrutiny, bad decisions are harder to catch and reverse.While centralization enables quick decisions and provides the unified political will that reform programs require, the risks of power concentration are considerable, especially since they strike directly at the foundations of the diversification project itself. When decisionmaking is reduced to a small circle of people shielded from scrutiny, bad decisions are harder to catch and reverse. No institutional channel exists allowing outside voices to identify problems or challenge assumptions before costs become irreversible. The recurrent revisions made to flagship initiatives, such as Saudi Arabia’s NEOM, illustrate the cost of such a shortcoming. In systems where major projects are overseen by a single leader, the reasons behind major reversals or modifications in projects are never fully transparent, and there is little accountability for wasted public funds or the fate of communities that may have been displaced by the projects.60A further risk is that when political and economic powers are fused, the conditions for genuine market competition can become compromised, with investment decisions reflecting political considerations rather than efficiency or long-term productivity. This is fertile ground for the approval of expensive projects that ultimately become liabilities. Lack of competition also stifles innovation and prevents efficient small and medium enterprises from growing and taking market shares from the established corporate sector. If returns in the private sector lag behind expectations and political freedoms are constrained, the most mobile and skilled nationals—precisely those upon whom successful diversification plans depend—will have strong incentives to leave. To be successful, diversification cannot afford to lose the people it most needs.Fundamentally, a vibrant private sector requires rule of law, secure property rights, and investor confidence. The tension between power concentration and private-sector dynamism was most clearly demonstrated in the detention of prominent Saudi businessmen at the Ritz-Carlton Hotel in Riyadh in 2017. Framed as an anti-corruption campaign, in which those arrested had to pay large sums of money or hand over property to be released, the move was widely interpreted as an attempt by Mohammed bin Salman to concentrate power.61 Whatever the intent, the episode signaled that property rights were not guaranteed by law and were subject to political discretion—at precisely the moment investor confidence was most urgently needed.62Alongside power consolidation, GCC governments have worked to build new bases of legitimacy that do not rely on the redistributive logic of the old social contract, and do not require expanding political participation. Two instruments have been central to this shift, namely new nationalisms and selective social liberalization. Within Gulf countries, nationalism anchored in the leadership of ruling figures and tied directly to their reform programs has gradually displaced other forms of identity, including pan-Islamist or pan-Gulf identities. In Saudi Arabia, this has taken a populist twist. For example, the Ritz-Carlton crackdown was welcomed by many young Saudis as a long-overdue reckoning with the privileges afforded the country’s elites, an attitude those behind the campaign encouraged.63 In parallel, social liberalization has expanded personal freedoms meaningfully, so that women can now drive and work with fewer restrictions, mixed-gender entertainment venues exist, and religious policing has been curtailed. While these changes are real, it remains unclear whether they can compensate for the material losses resulting from replacing the old rentier system, or the restrictions placed on political expression.Middle-Income Countries, the Pressure on Social Contracts, and the Reform TrapMiddle-income hydrocarbon exporters and importers occupy different positions in the regional political economy than the GCC countries, but also a more precarious one. Unlike the GCC states, which are attempting, however imperfectly, to move to a new pact with its society, governments in middle-income countries face a starker situation. The political economy of transformation in the MENA region is also shaped by regional interdependencies and geopolitical dynamics beyond the control of any individual government in the region.The Effect of Regional and Global Dynamics on Diversification EffortsThe economic transformation of the Middle East and North Africa will be influenced not only by decisions made within countries, but also by the regional and global context in which those decisions are made. Durable stability will require a more cooperative security framework that combines deterrence with diplomacy, reduces regional rivalries, and builds state institutions rather than undermining them.The Oil Transition TrapThe evolution of global hydrocarbon demand, shaped by market dynamics and geopolitical disruptions, will be decisive in determining the MENA region’s ability to sustain economic transformation. As the global energy landscape shifts, the central challenge for exporters will be to navigate a narrowing window of opportunity in maintaining oil and gas revenues while accelerating the transition toward diversified, productive, and resilient economic models.106 As the energy transition advances and global oil demand growth slows, plateaus, and eventually declines, oil exporters will face mounting pressure to adapt to an increasingly competitive and volatile market environment.
