Yet if several producers were to adopt such an approach simultaneously, it would mean moving toward a competitive global energy market that could accelerate a decline in hydrocarbon prices, with revenues converging in the longer term toward marginal production costs. This would result in a lose-lose outcome for producers, undermining fiscal stability and weakening diversification efforts.108The strategic calculations of energy producers regarding the future of energy markets   underscore a central tension: Even as competition intensifies, coordination among producers remains essential. Managing output collectively will be critical if these countries are to stabilize revenues and preserve the financial resources needed to fund economic transformations. At the same time, geopolitical instability in the Middle East, particularly disruptions to energy infrastructure and maritime routes, will likely accelerate the global energy transition, putting pressure on producers to speed up the diversification of their economies.109 Recurrent supply shocks and heightened risk perceptions are pushing major Asian importers, the main drivers of future hydrocarbon demand with around 40 percent of their oil imports transiting through the Strait of Hormuz, to diversify energy sources, accelerate investments in renewable energy, and reduce dependency on Middle Eastern hydrocarbons (see figure 14).110 This, in turn, could hasten a structural decline in oil and gas demand, exacerbating competition among exporters.The relationship between the global energy transition and economic diversification is therefore bidirectional. Countries that succeed in diversifying their economies will be better positioned to adopt flexible, forward-looking hydrocarbon strategies and manage the impact of this transition smoothly. By contrast, those that remain dependent on hydrocarbon revenues may be driven toward short-term revenue maximization that would reinforce market volatility and potentially accelerate the global shift away from fossil fuels. The implications are profound. If oil and gas prices weaken steadily due to declining demand or oversupply, per capita income in hydrocarbon producing economies could fall significantly in the coming decades. This would intensify political and social strains, making economic diversification away from hydrocarbons both urgent and more difficult. For hydrocarbon exporting countries, it’s better to anticipate change than be forced to react to it.Regional Integration and the MENA Region’s Place in the Global EconomyFor several reasons, regional integration is essential for advancing structural economic reforms and improving the Middle East and North Africa’s insertion into the global economy. First, the region remains among the world’s least economically integrated despite decades of economic liberalization.111 A larger, more integrated regional market would help the countries diversify their economies by combining the Gulf’s financial resources with the labor force, industrial capacities, and entrepreneurial potential of middle-income economies. Greater integration can generate new complementarities in investment, production, and supply chains, and countries would therefore be able to take advantage of each other’s comparative advantages rather than work in fragmented national markets. It would also boost the region’s collective economic power, giving it greater leverage to negotiate trade and investment agreements with major partners such as the United States, the European Union, and Asian economies.Second, building on regional integration could help channel more of the region’s financial wealth back into regional economies. For decades, much Gulf capital has been invested in Europe and North America. But the rise in geopolitical tensions and the increasing uncertainty about the treatment of sovereign assets abroad have highlighted the benefits of investing closer to home. If more of the Gulf’s assets were invested in the MENA region, it could have a transformational effect on recipient countries, giving them an incentive to pursue reform agendas. There has been a shift in Gulf financial engagement in the region over the past several years, a trend that will undoubtedly persist as the GCC’s diversification plans move forward. The era of relatively unconditional assistance to highly indebted countries such as Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan, and Lebanon in the form of budget deposits, aid, and other forms of assistance is over and has been replaced by a more selective approach.112 Gulf governments have been moving away from direct budgetary support to asset acquisition and investments in key sectors such as infrastructure, energy, agriculture, and renewable energy.113 This shift changes the dynamics between investors and recipient countries. Gulf investments are being directed at bankable projects and participation in strategic sectors. This is compelling recipient countries to improve the business environment, reform state-owned enterprises, and improve economic governance.114 The challenge down the road will be to turn Gulf investment into a driver of regional integration. Greater transparency, clearer norms, and regional institutional mechanisms could help align investments with development strategies, thereby harnessing financial flows in order to expand regional economic integration.Third, many of the region’s most urgent challenges are shared problems that transcend national boundaries. Water scarcity, climate change, environmental degradation, food security, and the return of refugees and displaced populations are problems of common concern and cannot be addressed effectively through isolated national policies. They need to be coordinated, planned jointly, and addressed collectively. In the near term, among the region’s most urgent priorities will be rebuilding countries shattered by conflict and enabling displaced people to return home. The way in which Gaza, Syria, Lebanon, and Yemen are rebuilt will affect the lives of millions of people, but also the economic and political future of the region.Israel’s participation in such a regional economic framework will depend on progress toward a resolution of the Palestinian question, which is crucial to broader regional acceptance and cooperation. Addressing these common regional challenges requires building adequate institutions. A MENA bank for reconstruction and development can serve as a platform to anchor regional integration in concrete projects.115 An institution of this kind could steer investment toward long-term priorities such as infrastructure, climate resilience, and post-conflict reconstruction. Without institutions to support such longer-term objectives, it will be difficult to lay the groundwork for lasting economic transformation and regional stability.A MENA bank for reconstruction and development can serve as a platform to anchor regional integration in concrete projects.Lastly, securing trade routes and improving regional connectivity are inherently collective enterprises. Recent tensions with Iran have highlighted the vulnerability of key maritime chokepoints, particularly the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab, and have accelerated efforts to develop alternative transport and energy corridors (see figure 15). Governments in the Gulf are seeking to bolster economic resilience by investing in projects that connect their countries to the Levant and Türkiye through railways, pipelines, ports, and logistics networks.116 In this context, deeper regional integration is an important driver of growth and increasingly an important element of economic security.
However, regional integration should not be confined to the Arab world. It must also involve Türkiye and Iran in order to have a transformative and pacifying impact. Economic integration can help ease regional tensions by creating common interests and mutual dependencies based on prosperity.117 A stable regional order will require an inclusive framework that incorporates all major regional players into cooperative arrangements. Türkiye and Iran have large domestic markets and industrial capacities and enjoy strategic geographical locations, while the Gulf countries have major financial resources and investment capacity. These assets together could unlock new trade, investment, and industrial development opportunities across the region. But realizing this potential will demand political deescalation and sustained efforts to build trust between Iran and its Arab neighbors. Without such progress, the economic gains from regional integration are unlikely to be fully realized.The MENA region has undergone decades of economic liberalization, but these efforts have not translated into deeper regional integration or a stronger position in the global economy. Despite international trade agreements, such as the Euro-Mediterranean agreements linking several MENA countries to the European Union, the region plays a minor role in the global economy, limiting its ability to develop regional value chains, attract investment, and shape the terms of its engagement with global economic actors.118 Regional integration is a key and urgent step to rethinking the region’s global insertion in a world distinguished by growing geopolitical competition and the emergence of competing economic blocs. In this new environment characterized by protectionism, a return of tariffs, and global competition, building a regional bloc is essential to increasing the bargaining power of the states involved.Conclusion: Vicious or Virtuous Cycle?The MENA region is at a critical stage in its trajectory. The interaction between domestic reform pathways, regional developments, and wider geopolitical shifts will shape the region in the coming years. This will determine not only the success or failure of economic transformations within individual states, but also the prospective regional order. The central question is whether the region will move toward greater stability, economic reform, and integration, or toward further fragmentation, insecurity, and cycles of economic decline.Structural tensions are building up across the region as a result of stagnant growth models, demographic pressures, climate vulnerabilities, fiscal constraints, and geopolitical tensions that can no longer be addressed through short-term crisis responses. In many countries, existing political and economic arrangements will deepen vicious cycles that shaped outcomes for much of the past decade. Economic stagnation has created social frustration, which undermines legitimacy, leading to political instability, which discourages investment and reform. This has led to rising unemployment, disenchantment, and conflict, and consequently to regional instability caused by a fear of uprisings. However, an alternative trajectory remains possible.If managed carefully, reformist momentum can create a virtuous cycle that might transform not only domestic political economies but also the regional order. Economic transformation must not be narrowly conceived as a technical process of economic diversification. Fundamentally, it is a political project that requires building new sources of legitimacy, new social contracts, and new regional arrangements facilitating cooperation. The challenge is common to all countries and requires moving from fragile, often rent-dependent economic systems to more productive and resilient economies. Yet each country needs to determine its path on its own, depending on its resources, institutional capacities, and political constraints.Economic transformation, whether toward more diversified economies in the case of energy-exporting countries or more productive ones for energy-importing countries, imposes difficult political choices. Governments will have to build reform coalitions, manage resistance from vested interests, and redefine the role of the state. To secure long-term stability, they need to abandon short-termism and act strategically. Stability cannot be built indefinitely on the narrow logic of regime-survival or on fiscally unsustainable distributive mechanisms. Legitimacy must be rooted more in productivity, inclusion, open access to economic opportunities, and credible visions of development that can rally societies around a common national project. Four interlinked conditions will determine whether countries in the region choose to enter a virtuous cycle or perpetuate a vicious cycle: an ability to make reforms politically and socially acceptable; creating conditions for a new regional security architecture; advancing regional integration; and acting collectively as a constructive global actor.The first condition is ensuring the political and social acceptability of reforms. No matter how technically sound economic reforms are, they cannot succeed if they are perceived as being externally imposed and serving the narrow interests of elites. Reform agendas, therefore, need to be embedded in larger national narratives of economic sovereignty, national security, and collective prosperity. Societies must see reforms as part of a long-term project of transformation, rather than as sacrifices imposed to preserve existing political systems. Therefore, strengthening state capacity to design, coordinate, and implement lasting development policies is essential, as states are the primary actors responsible for driving and sustaining reforms. Transformations are possible only with planning capacity, credible institutions, and the ability to design coherent sequencing of policies and compensation mechanisms. Knowledge ecosystems can play an important role in this area: think tanks, research institutes, universities, and policy networks can contribute to the development of strategic visions, policy expertise, and elite consensus on enduring priorities.It is also important to build broad reform coalitions. Economic elites, the middle class, labor groups, and the younger generations need to see that they have a stake in the transformation process. Reforms perceived as being socially unjust or politically exclusionary are likely to generate contestation, deepen distrust, and encourage defensive responses from societies and regimes. Regimes will be more concerned with survival than with structural transformation. This ultimately degrades economic situations and makes political systems fragile over time.The second condition that helps determine whether regional countries can enter a virtuous cycle is the creation of a new regional security architecture. However, there are major hurdles in doing so. Perceptions of threat vary widely among the Gulf states, including in relation to Iran and Israel. Some countries view Israel as a possible security partner in dealing with Iran, while others fear that Israeli regional dominance could itself be destabilizing. At the same time, competing security approaches have been increasingly defining the region. The UAE is deepening its ties with India and Israel, while Saudi Arabia seems to be increasingly interested in working with Türkiye and Pakistan. Meanwhile, Iranian influence in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen continues to fuel regional tensions. Egypt, in turn, is walking a tightrope between Emirati and Saudi strategic orientations, juggling its financial dependence on both countries and its security priorities. These competing security alignments might escalate and produce a fractured, unstable regional security landscape. Intra-Gulf rivalries, unresolved tensions with Iran, and competing external alliances could prove especially destabilizing, diverting resources away from development and generating cycles of insecurity. However, if a stable regional security order can arise, it could significantly encourage cooperation, investment, and long-term economic transformation.The third condition is enhanced regional integration. Economic integration is not only desirable but also structurally necessary if diversification and economic transformation strategies are to succeed. Trade integration must be complemented by broader reforms to improve the business environment, reduce bureaucratic red tape, strengthen competition, modernize customs systems, and improve infrastructural connectivity. Lowering transportation and logistical costs and improving the efficiency of border procedures will increase trade integration and participation in global value chains.119In contrast, the absence of regional integration will anchor the region in its current vicious cycle. Continued political rivalries, weak trade connectivity, and limited economic cooperation will constrain efforts to build diversified and productive economies by denying countries access to larger markets. They will also discourage investment in a region suffering from chronically low investment levels. Fragmented markets and persistent insecurity, in turn, will exacerbate domestic political fragilities, reinforcing economic stagnation and geopolitical competition.The fourth condition that will determine whether countries can enter into a virtuous cycle involves the region’s relations with the global order. The MENA region needs to become, collectively, a constructive global actor rather than a geopolitical battleground. This means creating regional institutions and mechanisms that can address transnational challenges such as migration, refugees, climate change, state fragility, and reconstruction of conflict areas. The absence of such mechanisms has contributed to a perception of the region as being chronically unstable and unable to manage collective problems.The MENA region needs to become, collectively, a constructive global actor rather than a geopolitical battleground.The comparison with Southeast Asia is instructive. Despite their political differences and a history of conflict, leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations understood that cooperation would increase stability, shared prosperity, and collective bargaining power. This is not the case in the MENA region, which is perceived globally as made up of rich yet fragile states that fail to cooperate and have been unable to articulate a shared vision for the future. The region’s exposure to external influence, coupled with the enduring legacy of colonialism, which is still present given Israel’s settler colonialism and occupation of Arab lands, has undermined prospects for meaningful regional cooperation and playing a beneficial global role. Changing this perception is not simply a matter of regional branding, even though many Gulf countries have invested heavily in entertainment, sports, tourism, and other forms of soft power to burnish their international profile. Rather, there should be an effort to make the region a “good” global actor—in other words able to manage internal conflict, build mechanisms for cooperation despite divergent interests, and work collectively to address common challenges. This means taking responsibility for the region’s future rather than waiting for external powers to intervene, and preventing internal crises from breeding instability that affects the rest of the world.All this will be essential for the MENA region’s ability to negotiate internationally and position itself within future global transformations, such as the energy transition, the AI revolution, the end of American unilateralism, and the emergence of a multipolar world.About the Commission MembersMuna Abbas, Chief Executive Officer, Asfari FoundationMohammed Abdel Raouf, Director of the Environmental Security and Sustainability Research Program, Gulf Research Center.Abdulkhaleq Abdulla, Expert at the Emirates Center for Strategic Studies and Research (ECSSR) and Visiting Professor at Harvard University.Youssef Al-Ebraheem, former Minister of Finance of KuwaitZiad BahaEddin, Egyptian economist and lawyer, former Deputy Prime Minister for Economic Development and Minister of International Cooperation.Ferid Belhaj, former World Bank Vice President for the Middle East and North Africa.Noha El Mikawy, former Dean of the School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, American University in Cairo.Rima Khalaf, former UN Under-Secretary-General and Executive Secretary of ESCWAAli Kooli, banker, former Minister of Economy, Finance and Investment Support of TunisiaSlim Othmani, Algerian businessman and former Chairman of NCA-Rouiba and President of the Algerian think tank CARETarik Youssef, Senior Fellow, Middle East Council on Global AffairsMaha Yahya, Director, Malcolm H.
